doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23

title: Camp Beauregard band in World War I
summary: Laine was sent for to organize an Army band at Camp Beauregard, stayed about seven weeks, then quit music.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Yes. Yes, exactly. This bugbearer played. Exactly. I said, look here. I said, that ain't my stuff. Nothing in the world is. Same stuff to that thing. Now, I quit playing music right after War I, first war. Not some of them, most of them were drafted. One of them died in the Army. Well, they took some of the boys up there like, I'm going to explain it to you, and they made a band up there, you know. At the camp? Yeah, at the camp. At the camp. At the camp Beauregard. They sent down for me. And I was right busy, playing right along. So, they sent down for me. But I had a few extra men on the side. And I had to keep some of them jobs going. You understand why? Oh, most of them were gone. Yeah. Good luck, I used to have a few spares, don't you know, that I could fall on. Well, I went up there. They asked me to come up there. I went up there, you know. And I don't know what the major's name was anyhow. But no, anyway, they sent me my ticket. They sent me $50 a week in cake. All right, I went up there and I stayed up there for about seven weeks or something like that. And I couldn't stay any longer. So, just before I left, maybe a day or two, they were speaking about Armistice. You understand? But I left. And after that they did. They closed the place and turned it into a nigger camp. And they'd get you a colored camp. We used to make all kinds of money. We'd play for them while they were in the mess room. We'd play. We'd play for dances for them. One of the crazy boogers would put their hats out, you know. Make us dimes quartered and all that matter. We'd share. After we got done playing, we'd share $80, $10 a piece. That went on until I came back and kept playing with my band, you see. There was a couple that I had left, you see. And I stopped. And so I couldn't make the go, I stopped. All my good men were gone.
